title: Two thousand concurrent workers
subtitle: Load-testing the memory and code-intelligence service with a fleet of AI agents on one workstation, with zero failures
technologies: Capacity engineering, backpressure and load testing
Code graph and static dependency analysis

stats.label: concurrent AI workers on the retrieval tools at once
requests a second held in keyword mode, from a floor of 1,271

lede: Every agent in my estate asks the memory service before it acts: what did we decide, what calls this symbol, how does this path work. If that service stalls under a fleet, every agent stalls with it. So I load-tested it the way the fleet uses it: two thousand concurrent AI workers hammering the retrieval tools at once, on a single workstation. Nothing failed. One workstation: a 24-core Intel Core Ultra with 256 GB of DDR5 and a consumer Blackwell GPU that was not used to accelerate retrieval. The service is Rust over PostgreSQL. Semantic search ran at about 1.2 seconds median across a working codebase. Every endpoint is bounded. The reranker saturates rather than errors under load.
quote: The slow row is honest: code search over a large index at two thousand concurrent callers is bound by the database, and the numbers say so.
evidence: Load testing with AI agent fleets: 2,000 concurrent AI workers on a memory and code-intelligence service on one workstation, with 0 failures.
Capacity engineering and backpressure: every endpoint bounded, a reranker that saturates instead of erroring, and a dedicated pool so observation writes never compete with reads.
Retrieval service performance: 1,479 requests a second held in keyword mode from a floor of 1,271; repeat questions answered from cache in under 100 milliseconds.
Rust and PostgreSQL service design: a precomputed code graph, so a dependency trace under load is a bounded traversal rather than a model call.
author: Corey James
